readings.c1s2:
¶
'''unburiable''' (un-ber′i-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being buried; unfit to be buried. ''Tennyson'', Gareth and Lynette.

'''unburied''' (un-ber′id), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unburied''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''buried''.] Not buried; not interred.
{{smaller block|The dead carcasses of ''unburied'' men.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iii. 3. 122.}}}}

'''unburned, unburnt''' (un-bėrnd′, un-bėrnt′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unbrent''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''burned'', ''burnt''.] '''1.''' Not burned; not consumed or injured by fire.
{{smaller block|<poem>He said ’twas folly,
For one poor grain or two, to leave ''unburnt'',
And still to nose the offence. ''Shak.'', Cor., v. 1. 27.</poem>
The source of the heat taken up by the vessel is nothing but ''unburnt'' gases. ''Sci. Amer. Supp.'', XXII. 8783.}}
'''2.''' Not baked, as brick.

'''unburning''' (un-bėr′ning), ''a.'' Not consuming away by fire. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The ''unburning'' fire called light.
{{right|''Sir K. Digby'', Of Bodies, vii.}}}}

'''unburnt''' (un-bėrnt′), ''a.'' See ''unburned.''
{{smaller block|O bush ''unbrent'', brenning in Moyses syghte.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prioress’s Tale, l. 16.}}}}

'''unburrow''' (un-bur′ō), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''burrow''<sup>2</sup>.] To take from a burrow; unearth. [Rare.]
readings.c1s3:
¶
{{smaller block|He can bring down sparrows and ''unburrow'' rabbits.
{{right|''Dickens'', Uncommercial Traveller, x. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unburthen''', ''v. t.'' See ''unburden.''

'''unbury''' (un-ber′i), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unburied'', ppr. ''unburying.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''bury''<sup>3</sup>.] '''1.''' To exhume; disinter. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The hours they are not at their beads, which are not a few, they employ in speaking ill of us, ''unburying'' our bones, and burying our reputations.
{{right|''Jarvis'', Don Quixote, II. iii. 5. (''Davies.'')}}}}
'''2.''' Figuratively, to uncover; reveal; disclose.
{{smaller block|<poem>Since you have one secret, keep the other;
Never ''unbury'' either.</poem>
{{right|''Lytton'', Richelieu, i. 1.}}}}

'''unbusinesslike''' (un-biz′nes-līk), ''a.'' Not businesslike.

'''unbutton''' (un-but′n), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''button.''] To unfasten or open, as a garment, by separating the buttons and the buttonholes.
{{smaller block|What is the life of man! Is it not to shift from side to side, from sorrow to sorrow?—to button up one cause of vexation, and ''unbutton'' another?
{{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, iv. 31.}}}}

'''unbuxom†''' (un-buk′sum), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unbuxom, unbuxum, unboxum, unbuhsum''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''buxom.''] Disobedient. ''Piers Plowman'' (C), iii. 87.

'''unbuxomly†''' (un-buk′sum-li), ''adv.'' In a disobedient manner. ''Gower'', Conf. Amant., i.

'''unbuxomness†''' (un-buk′sum-nes), ''n.'' [< ME. *''unbuxomnes, unbuxsumnes''; < ''unbuxom'' + ''-ness.''] Disobedience.
{{smaller block|<poem>Sen Lucifer oure ledar es lighted so lawe
For hys ''vnbuxumnes'' in bale to be brente.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 6.}}}}
readings.c1s4:
¶
'''uncabled''' (un-kā′bld), ''a.'' Not fastened or secured by a cable.
{{smaller block|Within it ships . . . ''uncabled'' ride secure.
{{right|''Cowper'', Odyssey, xiii. 117.}}}}

'''uncage''' (un-kāj′), ''v. t.'' To set free from a cage or from confinement.
{{smaller block|The ''uncaged'' soul flew through the air.
{{right|''Fanshaw'', Poems (ed. 1676), p. 299.}}}}
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''uncarnate''' (un-kär′nāt), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''carnate.''] To divest of flesh or fleshliness. ''Bp. Gauden.'' [Rare.]

'''uncart''' (un-kärt′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''cart.''] To unload or discharge from a cart. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He carted and ''uncarted'' the manure with a sort of flunkey grace.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Amos Barton, ii. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''uncase''' (un-kās′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''case''<sup>2</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To take out of a case; release from a case or covering: especially (''milit.'') used of the colors or any portable flag; hence, to disclose; reveal.
{{smaller block|Commit securely to true wisdome the vanquishing and ''uncasing'' of craft and sutletie.
{{right|''Milton'', Ref. in Eng., ii.}}}}
'''2.''' To strip; flay; case. See ''case''<sup>2</sup>.
{{smaller block|<poem>The Foxe, first Author of that treacherie,
He did ''uncase'', and then away let flie.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Mother Hub. Tale, l. 1380.}}}}
'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To undress. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Do you not see Pompey is ''uncasing'' for the combat?
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 707.}}}}

'''uncastle''' (un-kȧs′l), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''castle.''] '''1.''' To deprive of a castle; turn out of a castle. ''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., III. ii. 39. (''Davies.'')—'''2.''' To deprive of the distinguishing marks or appearances of a castle. ''Fuller.'' [Rare in both uses.]

'''uncate''' (ung′kāt), ''a.'' [< LL. ''uncatus'', hooked, curved, < L. ''uncus'', a hook: see ''unce''<sup>2</sup>, ''uncus.''] Same as ''uncinate.''

'''uncathedraled, uncathedralled''' (un-kạ-thē′drald), ''a.'' Destitute of cathedrals. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|If he [Longfellow] had, like Whittier, grown old among the ''uncathedralled'' paganisms of American scenery and life, etc.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XIV. 862.}}}}
readings.c3s4:
¶
'''uncaused''' (un-kâzd′), ''a.'' Having no precedent cause; existing without an author; uncreated; self-existent.
{{smaller block|The idea of ''uncaused'' matter. {{right|''Baxter'', On the Soul, ii. 359.}}}}

'''uncautelous†''' (un-kâ′te-lus), ''a.'' Incautious.

'''uncautious''' (un-kâ′shus), ''a.'' Incautious. ''Dryden'', Pal. and Arc., ii. 74.

'''uncautiously''' (un-kâ′shus-li), ''adv.'' Incautiously. ''Waterland.''

'''unce<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' A Middle English variant of ''ounce''<sup>1</sup>.

'''unce<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' [< L. ''uncus'', a hook, barb; cf. ''uncus'', hooked, barbed, bent: see ''Uncaria.''] A claw.
{{smaller block|<poem>The river-walking serpent to make sleepe,
Whose horrid crest, blew skales, and ''unces'' blacke,
Threat every one a death.</poem>
{{right|''Heywood'', Brit. Troy, vii. 76. (''Nares.'')}}}}

Severe, as a fall or blow. {{smaller block|An ''uncanny'' coup I gat for my pains. {{right|''Scott'', Waverley, lxvi.}}}} '''uncanonic''' (un-ka̤-non′ik), ''a.'' Same as ''uncanonical.'' {{smaller block|This act was ''uncanonic'' and a fault. {{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, II. 170.}}}} '''uncanonical''' (un-ka̤-non′i-kal), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not canonical; not agreeable to the canons. {{smaller block|If ordinations were ''uncanonical.'' {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Episcopacy Asserted, § 32.}}}} '''2.''' Not conformed or conforming to rule; not determined by rule.—'''3.''' Not belonging to the canon (of Scripture).—'''Uncanonical hours.''' {{smaller|See ''hour.''}} '''uncanonicalness''' (un-ka̤-non′i-kal-nes), ''n.'' The character of being uncanonical. ''Bp. Lloyd.'' '''uncanonized''' (un-kan′ọn-īzd), ''a.'' Not canonized; not enrolled among the saints. {{smaller block|The members of it [the Romish communion] boast very much of mighty signs and wonders wrought by some canonized and some ''uncanonized'' saints. {{right|''Bp. Atterbury'', Sermons, II. i.}}}} '''uncap''' (un-kap′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''uncapped'', ppr. ''uncapping''. [< ''un-''2 + ''cap''1.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To remove a cap, as a percussion-cap, from, as a gun or a cartridge, or a protecting cap from, as a lens-tube. '''II.''' ''intrans.'' To remove the cap or hat. {{smaller block|I felt really like ''uncapping'', with a kind of reverence. {{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Trans. Sketches, p. 247.}}}} '''uncapable†''' (un-kā′pa-bl), ''a.'' Incapable. {{smaller block|An inhuman wretch, ''Uncapable'' of pity. {{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iv. 1. 5.}} He who came to take away the sins of the world was ''uncapable'' of pollution by sin. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, V. 176.}}}} '''uncape''' (un-kāp′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''2 + ''cape''2.] In ''hawking'', to prepare for flying at game by taking off the cape or hood. {{smaller|Various explanations are given to the word as used by Shakspere, “Merry Wives,” iii. 3. 176: “I warrant we’ll unkennel the fox. Let me stop this way first. ''a'', corolla laid open; ''b'', calyx-tube laid open, showing the style and stigma; ''c'', fruit with persistent calyx.}}}} of gamopetalous plants, of the order ''Rubiaceæ'' and tribe ''Naucleeæ.'' {{smaller|It is distinguished from the type-genus ''Nauclea'' by its valvate corolla and septicidal capsule.
